senses: The political ideology of being a citizen in a state as a republic under which the people hold popular sovereignty.
The identification of geographic location, as of an electronic device or an animal being tracked.
The latitude and longitude coordinates of a particular location. Term and definition standardized by ISO/IEC 19762-5:2008 (this standard has since been revised by ISO/IEC 19762:2016).
A low-level flight of a ceremonial nature; a flyover (US)
examples: An impromptu flypast by the Red Arrows finished off the special event in style.

senses: A shrine of offerings to one's ancestors set up on the Day of the Dead.
examples: Other marginalized groups draw attention to their cause through large public ofrendas that usually include pictorial or sculptural and sometimes literary calaveras.
This show featured installations, painting, and sculptures, all of which are recast as ofrendas to the dead.

senses: A fast military offensive, typically involving a large and highly mobile tank force with air support.
Sudden activity; a flurry.
ety: Unadapted borrowing from German Blitzkrieg (literally “lightning war”).
examples: I rode a tank, held a general's rank / When the Blitzkrieg raged and the bodies stank
President-elect Donald Trump has promised a blitzkrieg of executive actions and legislation after he takes office Jan. 20.

senses: skin swelling or sore; blister; blotch.
ety: From Middle English blein, from Old English bleġen, bleġene, from Proto-Germanic *blajinǭ, *blajjinǭ, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel- (“to swell up”). Cognate with West Frisian blein (“blain”), Dutch blein, blegn (“blain”), Middle Low German bleine (“blain”). Related also to dialectal Norwegian bleime (“blister”), Old Swedish blēma (“blister”), French bleime (“an inflammation of a horse's hoof”).

senses: A legendary creature, human male from the waist up, fishlike from the waist down.
ety: From Middle English mereman, from Old English *meremann (“merman”) (suggested by Old English meremenn, meremennen, meremenin (“mermaid, siren”)), equivalent to mer- + man. Cognate with Dutch meerman (“merman”), German Meermann (“merman”).

senses: Japanese or Korean food that is dipped in flour and then deep-fried, typically made from boneless chicken.
ety: Borrowed from Japanese 唐揚げ (karaage). Likely from 唐 (kara-, “Chinese, foreign”) + 揚げ (age, “deep-fried food”), although the etymology of kara is disputed.

senses: Of a coast or shore, without bays.
Having the power or authority to make decisions.
examples: The procedures should also make plain that a decisional official, whether or not challenged, may voluntarily abstain from participating in a particular proceeding.

senses: Cleft; divided into two principal or main parts, such as two lobes.
ety: From Latin bifidus (“divided in two”), from bi- (“two”) + -fidus, combining form of findere (“to split”).

senses: The bag inside a vacuum cleaner where collected dust is stored.
A bag in which clothing can be protected from damage.
examples: These may contain filters manufactured without the use of harmful materials and may not require a dustbag. Dyson vacuum cleaners are examples of designs with such characteristics.

senses: Having a red colour; reddish
A government run by idiots.
ety: From idiot + -cracy. The word was coined by the writers of a 2006 movie about the topic, which some have interpreted as presaging, through caricature, the state of the world.

senses: Suitable for heating in a microwave oven; said of food and non-food items, especially containers.
A traditional administrative unit of the Minangkabau people of West Sumatra, Indonesia, consisting of a cluster of villages.
ety: From Indonesian nagari, ultimately from Sanskrit नगरी (nagarī, “city”).

senses: A soft, legless larva of a fly or other dipteran insect, that often eats decomposing organic matter.
ety: From Middle English magot, magat, maked, probably a metathetic alteration of maddock, maðek (“worm", "maggot”), originally a diminutive form of a base represented by Old English maþa (Scots mathe), from Proto-West Germanic *maþō, from Proto-Germanic *maþô, from the Proto-Indo-European root *mat, which was used in insect names, equivalent to made + -ock. Near-cognates include Dutch made, German Made and Swedish mask, Icelandic maðkur (“worm, grub, maggot”). senses: A butler or majordomo in Spain or Latin America.
ety: From Spanish mayordomo. Doublet of majordomo.

senses: A colloid gel in which water is the continuous phase; they have a number of medical and industrial applications.
Any structure consisting of two layers of molecules
The belief in or practice of going nude in social, nonsexualized and frequently mixed-gender groups specifically in cultures where going nude in the social situation is not the norm.
ety: From French nudisme. By surface analysis, nude + -ism.

senses: More generally, consisting of two metals.
ety: From French bimétallique. Equivalent to bi- + metallic.

senses: A defile or narrow gorge, especially one that cuts transversely through the rock of an otherwise continuous ridge.
ety: In many cases, italicized as a borrowing of French cluse. In Early Modern texts, possibly a continuation of Middle English cluse, Old English clūse (“narrow pass”).

senses: A person who operates a snowmobile.
Making up for deficiencies; supplementary; suppletory.
An unusually low sale price, typically offered by a retailer on a limited number of items for a limited time, often on prominent shopping days, such as the day after Thanksgiving in the US.
ety: From door + buster, suggesting that customers would stampede through the doors of the retailer.

senses: A stew of Ethiopia and Eritrea origin whose primary ingredient is powdered chickpeas or broad-bean meal.
ety: Possibly from Amharic or Tigrinya ሺሮ (širo, “chickpea flour”)

senses: Something that hydrates.
A compartment or drawer, as in a refrigerator, for keeping perishable foods fresh and preventing moisture loss.
Having a value or cost of tenpence.
Something or someone that is shorter than normal.
A person employed to sort.
A machine or algorithm that performs sorting.
Able to be depreciated.
A solid, waxy, flammable substance of a dull gray to blackish color, formed within the intestines of the sperm whale and used in the production of perfumes.
ety: From Old French ambre gris (“grey amber”). Though the term was initially spaced as two words, single-word forms predominated by the 19th century. In the 17th century, folk etymologies interpreting the term as amber grease or amber [of] Greece enjoyed some popularity.

senses: Something that ties, a ligature.
The act of tying, of applying a ligature.
The state of having a ligature, of being tied.
ety: Borrowed from Late Latin ligatio, ligationis, from Latin ligo. Doublet of liaison.

senses: A system for determining the position of vessels lost at sea by means of explosive sounds.
ety: Shortened from sound fixing and ranging. Compare sonar.

senses: A traditional Polish stew containing cabbage and meat
examples: I bombarded him with questions about his history with bigos.

senses: The quality or state of being metallic.
Painful, excruciating, torturing.
ety: From Middle English torterous, from Anglo-Norman torturous, from Old French tortureus, from Latin tortūra. By surface analysis, torture + -ous.

senses: Any dramatic change from one thing to another
One who, or that which, shells.
